reconcile.connective: These expositors treat the four reports as naming one and the same placard, lining up the evangelists' varying terms and citing the fullest Johannine form.

discrepancy.connective: Thomas Paine pressed the four wordings as proof the evangelists disagreed and so could not have been eyewitnesses to the scene.

skeptic.name: Thomas Paine
skeptic.work: The Age of Reason, Part II
skeptic.attribution: Thomas Paine (d. 1809), The Age of Reason, Part II (1795)

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: The Evangelist John calls it a “title”, Joh 19:19, and Luke, a “superscription”, Luk 23:38, and Mark, the “superscription of his accusation”, Mar 15:26, it was what contained the sum and substance of what he was accused, and for which he was condemned, and suffered.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill harmonizes the four evangelists' differing labels for the placard by treating them as one inscription holding the same 'sum and substance' of the accusation, dissolving the wording difference.

excerpts.author: Matthew Henry
excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Matthew called it, aitia - the accusation; Mark and Luke called it epigraphē - the inscription; John calls it by the proper Latin name, titlos - the title: and it was this, Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews,
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Henry lines up the evangelists' varying terms for the same placard and gives the fullest Johannine form, treating the divergent reports as one title rather than conflicting wordings.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats the titulus among the gospel discrepancies, holding that the four evangelists give the inscription in varying terms and degrees of fullness while preserving one common charge.

link.note: Live apologetic treatment of this exact passage; argues the multilingual sign and partial-but-complementary quotations account for the four wordings.
